single.question: Can seeds survive immersion in sea-water?

memories.memory: I shared my final results on how long seeds can withstand immersion in sea-water. For example, Capsicum seeds did well after 137 days, Celery seeds, however, fared poorly, and Spinach seeds germinated well after 120 days. Different varieties of the same species reacted differently; for example, Broccoli seeds thrived after 11 days but were killed by 22 days, and Cauliflower seeds survived up to 36 days' immersion.

I have begun making some experiments on immersion in sea-water and the germinating powers of seeds, in the hope of understanding the distribution of plants on outlying islands and the mainland. The results I have so far are too few and unimportant to mention.

I observed that out of 23 kinds of seed, the five Leguminosæ were the only ones killed, except for the Cabbage seed, which survived in the ice-cold water. This suggests some seeds can survive immersion in sea-water.
I have begun some experiments on seeds to determine their susceptibility to sea-water, particularly interested in the kinds you might expect to be easily killed by it.
I found that the cress and lettuce seeds vegetated well after 21 days of immersion.

single.thinking: Nothing I have written before bears on this directly.
single.reply: I have made some experiments on the germinating powers of seeds in sea-water, and have found that seeds of the Leguminosæ are killed by it, but I do not know whether the other seeds will not be affected by immersion in the sea.
